description: When one stage becomes several tasks, and what a decomposition must satisfy to be accepted into the graph.
why: A stage is a unit of accountability, not a unit of work. `DEV` for a payments change is one task in the graph and five people's work in reality, and a graph that cannot say so cannot schedule it, cannot parallelise it, and cannot show anyone where the change actually is.

The decomposition itself is judgement: which pieces, in what order, sharing which contracts. This repository does not simulate judgement. An agent proposes, and the organization validates and records -- the same split as everywhere else here.

derived.what: Split a stage by the artifacts it produces and the roles that own them, taken from policies/artifact-model.json.
derived.when: The stage produces artifacts owned by more than one role. Otherwise there is no split to derive and this refuses.
derived.why: A stage owing an ARCH and an SLO owes them to two different owners, and that is already written down. Deriving it is reading, not guessing.

proposed.what: An agent proposes concrete tasks against schemas/task-proposal.schema.json; the organization validates every rule below and grafts what survives.
proposed.invents: the decomposition, which is the part that requires judgement
proposed.when: Anything the derived mode cannot answer.
proposed.why: The alternative is a heuristic in Python pretending to be engineering judgement, which is the failure this repository is arranged against.

rules.means: The union of the children's `produces` must equal the parent's, exactly.
rules.why: A decomposition that drops an artifact turns a stage the organization owes into one nobody owes, and the definition of done still passes because it is evaluated on the parent.

rules.means: Every child's role is in the agent registry and can write the storage of every artifact it produces.
rules.why: The same check the artifact model is held to. A task assigned to a role that cannot produce its output is a task nobody can do.

rules.means: A child may raise its risk above the parent's; it may not lower it.
rules.why: Otherwise decomposing HIGH work into LOW pieces is a way to route around the model floor, the approval gates and the concurrency limits, one level down where nobody is looking.

rules.means: A child may depend only on its siblings, and the sibling graph must be acyclic.
rules.why: The parent already carries the change's dependencies. A child reaching outside its stage rewires the graph from inside a stage, where the person reading the graph will not look.

rules.means: Every predicate in a child's definition of done is a real predicate from the artifact model, called with the right number of arguments.
rules.why: An unparseable predicate is silently skipped by the evaluator, so an invented one is a definition of done that always passes.

rules.means: Between 2 and max_children tasks, and one level of decomposition only.
rules.why: A stage that needs more than this is not a stage that needs decomposing; it is a work item that was scoped wrong. Depth is bounded for the same reason every other loop here is.

rules.means: The parent keeps its definition of done and comes to depend on all of its children. Downstream tasks keep depending on the parent.
rules.why: The stage gate is the thing the rest of the graph was promised. Replacing the parent with its children would delete it, and every downstream dependency with it.

rules.means: If the stage owns a coupled surface, exactly one child must own it.
rules.why: The coupling policy gives each shared contract one owner. Decomposing a stage that owns one and assigning it to nobody deletes that guarantee at the moment the work becomes parallel, which is precisely when it starts to matter; assigning it to every child is the opposite mistake and serialises the split away.

not_enforceable: Whether the decomposition is any good. The rules below reject a decomposition that is incoherent with the graph; they cannot reject one that is merely poor. That is policies/decomposition-review.json, which is a review rather than a rule -- there is no metric for cohesion on a set of engineering tasks and there will not be one. This line used to say 'that is what the reviewer on the stage is for', and it was not true: every stage gate reviews the stage's artifact, not the split, and the stages most likely to synthesize have no reviewer at all.

dependency_inference.why: A decomposition is the moment new ordering appears -- several tasks that did not exist a second ago, some of them editing the same files. A tool that has to be invoked by hand at precisely that moment will be missed.

skippable.why: Skipping is legitimate -- a project may know its ordering better than a regex over its imports does -- but on high-risk work it is a decision, and a decision made by typing a flag that produces a warning is one nobody made.
